title_en: Xingyuan Company and Uni-Star Starbucks v. Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Branch — dispute over trademark infringement and unfair competition
ruling_gist_en: Using another person's well-known trademark as one's own enterprise name, if it is sufficient to cause relevant public to be confused or mistaken between the trademark registrant and the owner of the enterprise name, constitutes an act of 'causing other damage to the exclusive right to use a registered trademark' as stipulated in Article 52(5) of the Trademark Law, and shall bear infringement liability according to law.

星源公司、统一星巴克诉上海星巴克、上海星巴克分公司商标侵权及不正当竞争纠纷案

Guiding Case No. XXX (omitted in original)

**Ruling Summary**

Where a party uses another's well-known trademark as its own enterprise name, which is sufficient to cause relevant members of the public to be mistaken or confused as to whether the trademark registrant and the enterprise name owner are related or are the same market entity, such act falls within the conduct "causing other damage to the exclusive right to use a registered trademark" under Article 52(5) of the Trademark Law, and the infringer shall bear tort liability according to law.

**Plaintiff:** Starbucks Corporation, domiciled at Utah Ave. South, Seattle, Washington, United States of America.
**Legal Representative:** David M. Landau, Senior Vice President and Associate General Counsel of the company.

**Plaintiff:** Shanghai Uni-Starbucks Coffee Co., Ltd., domiciled at Huaihai Middle Road, Luwan District, Shanghai, People's Republic of China.
**Legal Representative:** Lin Cangsheng, Chairman of the company.

**Defendant:** Shanghai Starbucks Cafe Co., Ltd., domiciled at Hongqiao Road, Changning District, Shanghai, People's Republic of China.
**Legal Representative:** Zhuang Lizhi, Chairwoman of the company.

**Defendant:** Shanghai Starbucks Cafe Co., Ltd., Nanjing Road Branch, domiciled at East Nanjing Road, Huangpu District, Shanghai, People's Republic of China.
**Person in Charge:** Zhuang Lizhi.

Plaintiffs Starbucks Corporation (hereinafter "Starbucks Corp.") and Shanghai Uni-Starbucks Coffee Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Uni-Starbucks") filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court against Defendants Shanghai Starbucks Cafe Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Shanghai Starbucks") and Shanghai Starbucks Cafe Co., Ltd., Nanjing Road Branch (hereinafter "Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch") for trademark infringement and unfair competition.

Plaintiffs Starbucks Corp. and Uni-Starbucks alleged: Starbucks Corp. was founded in 1971 and opened its first "STARBUCKS" coffee shop in Seattle, USA in 1976. Starbucks Corp. adopted a unique and effective management and operation model, providing consumers with excellent products and quality services. After more than 30 years of development, Starbucks Corp. has become a world-renowned coffee chain enterprise, and "STARBUCKS" is a globally famous coffee brand.

In July 1976, Plaintiff Starbucks Corp. applied for and obtained its first "STARBUCKS" trademark in the United States, covering goods in Class 30 (coffee, coffee-based beverages, coffee beverages with milk, coffee flavorings, and biscuits, pastries, bread, etc.). Thereafter, Starbucks Corp. successively registered the "STARBUCKS" trademark, the "STARBUCKS COFFEE" word and design trademark in over 100 countries and regions worldwide, covering more than 20 classes of goods and services. From 1996 to 2003, Starbucks Corp. registered the "STARBUCKS" and "STARBUCKS COFFEE" word and design trademarks in Mainland China, covering more than 10 classes of goods and services, including Class 30 and Class 42 (restaurants, cafes, snack bars, fast-food restaurants, etc.). From 1999 to 2000, Starbucks Corp. registered the "星巴克" trademark in Mainland China, covering 5 classes of goods and services. The "STARBUCKS" trademark enjoys high reputation and good will worldwide and is a well-known trademark recognized and familiar to consumers. As the owner of the "STARBUCKS" trademark, Starbucks Corp. has registered the "STARBUCKS" trademark in many countries and regions globally and has continuously used the trademark without interruption.

In 1999, Plaintiff Starbucks Corp. entered the Mainland China market, and on March 2, 2000, Plaintiff Uni-Starbucks was established pursuant to authorization from Starbucks Corp. After its establishment, Uni-Starbucks successively opened numerous Starbucks coffee chain stores in prime locations in Shanghai, Hangzhou, Ningbo, and other cities. These coffee chain stores have achieved tremendous economic and social benefits in China. The "STARBUCKS," "星巴克," and the "STARBUCKS" word and design trademarks also enjoy extremely high reputation in China.

Plaintiffs Starbucks Corp. and Uni-Starbucks discovered that Defendant Shanghai Starbucks was established on March 9, 2000, adopting "星巴克" as its business name (enterprise name). Defendant Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch was established on July 1, 2003, under Shanghai Starbucks. Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch, in their coffee business at the Xianxia store and the Nanjing Road store, used marks identical or similar to the "STARBUCKS," "星巴克," and the "STARBUCKS" word and design trademarks on mobile light boxes, light boxes, seat partitions, coffee menus, invoices, cash register receipts, business cards, and other items.

Plaintiffs Starbucks Corp. and Uni-Starbucks argued that the six trademarks registered in Class 30 for goods and Class 42 for services, namely "STARBUCKS," "星巴克," and the "STARBUCKS" word and design trademarks (hereinafter collectively referred to as the "six trademarks, including 'STARBUCKS'"), as well-known trademarks, are entitled to protection under Chinese Trademark Law. Defendants Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch, knowing the extremely high reputation of the above trademarks, still adopted the "星巴克" trademark as a part of their enterprise name, prominently used the name on various items within their cafes, and commercially used marks identical or similar to the six trademarks, including "STARBUCKS." Their conduct clearly manifests an intent to "free-ride" on the plaintiffs' goodwill, which is sufficient to cause relevant members of the public to mistakenly believe that the defendants are affiliated with the plaintiffs, as owners of the "STARBUCKS" trademark, or to confuse the two as the same market entity, leading to confusion as to the source of goods and services. The defendants' conduct infringes upon the plaintiffs' trademark rights and constitutes unfair competition. Therefore, the plaintiffs requested: (1) a declaration that the six trademarks, including "STARBUCKS," registered by Starbucks Corp. are well-known trademarks; (2) an order that the defendants immediately cease the infringement of the exclusive rights to use the above registered trademarks and the unfair competition against the plaintiffs; (3) a declaration that the defendants' use of the "星巴克" mark in their enterprise name constitutes infringement of the plaintiffs' well-known "星巴克" trademark; (4) an order that the defendants cease using all graphics and marks identical or similar to the six trademarks, including "STARBUCKS," and cease using enterprise names containing the "星巴克" mark; (5) confiscation and destruction of the defendants' existing infringing items; (6) an order that the defendants publicly apologize to the plaintiffs and eliminate the adverse impact by publishing an apology statement in *Jiefang Daily* and *Xinmin Evening News*; (7) an award of RMB 500,000 in economic damages to the plaintiffs; and (8) an order that the defendants pay the plaintiffs' reasonable attorneys' fees and other expenses incurred in connection with this lawsuit, totaling RMB 560,000.

Plaintiffs Starbucks Corp. and Uni-Starbucks submitted the following evidence:

1. A set of trademark registration documents, indicating the registration status of the six trademarks, including "STARBUCKS," and related trademarks in Mainland China, the United States, and other countries and regions worldwide, to prove that the plaintiffs hold trademark rights in the six trademarks, including "STARBUCKS," and related trademarks.

2. A set of evidentiary materials showing that the six trademarks, including "STARBUCKS," constitute well-known trademarks, including the degree of awareness of the six trademarks and related trademarks among relevant members of the public, the duration and geographic scope of the plaintiffs' use and promotion of the above trademarks, records of protection of the above trademarks as well-known trademarks, and other factors contributing to their fame, to prove the well-known status of the above trademarks globally and in Mainland China.

3. Business registration materials for Defendants Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch, to prove that the "星巴克" mark used as the name in the defendants' registered enterprise name is identical to the plaintiffs' "星巴克" trademark.

4. A report in the August 1, 2003, issue of *Jiefang Daily*, stating that Mr. Mao, General Manager of Shanghai Starbucks, was interviewed by the newspaper and said that because he thought that the U.S. Starbucks Corporation had opened over 4,000 stores and the "星巴克" brand was good, he preemptively registered the "星巴克" mark in Shanghai. This evidence is used to prove the defendants' subjective intent to "free-ride."

5. Notarial certificate No. (2003) Hu Huang Yi Zheng Jing Zi No. 7486, issued by the First Notary Public Office of Huangpu District, Shanghai, to prove that the defendants used word and graphic marks similar to the plaintiffs' six trademarks, including "STARBUCKS," in their business operations.

6. Notarized sample surveys and media reports concerning the defendants' infringement, to prove that relevant members of the public were confused between the plaintiffs and the defendants with respect to the business entities and their goods and services, and that the defendants acted with malice.

7. Notarized statistics on the defendants' customer traffic, profit statistics since the defendants' opening, invoices and receipts for the plaintiffs' payments of attorneys' fees, notarization fees, and translation fees, to prove that the defendants should compensate the plaintiffs RMB 500,000 in economic damages and pay the plaintiffs' reasonable attorneys' fees and other expenses totaling RMB 560,000 incurred in connection with this lawsuit.

Defendants Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch argued: (1) The plaintiffs submitted notarized and legalized company registration documents showing that Starbucks Corp. was established on November 4, 1985, but the plaintiffs stated in their complaint that the company was founded in 1971 and registered its first "STARBUCKS" trademark in 1976. The plaintiffs submitted only copies of the trademark rights evidence for the "星巴克" and "STARBUCKS" trademarks registered in Mainland China, without providing originals. As for other evidence of rights, such as "STARBUCKS" trademarks registered abroad, the notarized documents and the documents being notarized were separated without any integrated marking. Therefore, such evidence should not be admitted according to law. Thus, the plaintiffs are not qualified holders of the rights. (2) The plaintiffs' addition of claims after the expiration of the evidentiary period violated legal provisions. (3) The plaintiffs' claims are not substantively sustainable. The Chinese "星巴克" trademark and the English "STARBUCKS" trademark are independent trademarks, and the latter is irrelevant to this case. The plaintiffs' "星巴克" mark is merely an ordinary trademark. Uni-Starbucks has been in business for only a short time—less than four years from its establishment to the filing of this lawsuit—and the public's degree of awareness of this trademark is very low. Therefore, the "星巴克" trademark is not a well-known trademark. (4) There is no legal basis for the plaintiffs' request that the defendants cease using enterprise names containing the "星巴克" mark. The defendants obtained the enterprise name right including "星巴克" on October 20, 1999, which is earlier than Starbucks Corp.'s acquisition of the "星巴克" trademark right. Therefore, the defendants' enterprise name right, as a legitimate right obtained earlier, should be protected. (5) The defendants' conduct does not constitute trademark infringement or unfair competition. In their business operations, the defendants have always used their full enterprise name without prominently using the "星巴克" mark, which does not infringe upon the plaintiffs' exclusive right to use the "星巴克" trademark. The defendants' use of coffee cup patterns in their store decorations constitutes lawful use. The design is clearly different from the plaintiffs' "mermaid figure" graphic trademark in terms of pattern composition and visual effect, and thus does not infringe upon that graphic trademark. Furthermore, when Shanghai Starbucks pre-approved the "星巴克" text as part of its enterprise name, the plaintiffs had not yet operated any cafe or coffee business under the name "星巴克" in Mainland China. In summary, the plaintiffs' claims should not be supported.

Defendants Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch submitted the following evidence:

1. A notice of pre-approval of the enterprise name for Shanghai Starbucks, to prove that the defendants' enterprise name was pre-approved on October 20, 1999.

2. A set of photographs, pictures, and other evidential materials to prove that the circular, green-background, white-text, ring-shaped graphic is a common logo used by cafes and is not distinctive.

3. Photographs published in *Jiefang Daily*, to prove that the plaintiffs' mermaid graphic trademark (i.e., the "STARBUCKS" word and design trademark) and the defendants' coffee cup pattern logo are clearly different and would not cause confusion.

4. Market usage survey reports, an application for cancellation of a registered trademark for non-use for three consecutive years, and other evidential materials, to show that after Starbucks Corp. obtained the exclusive right to use the "星巴克" trademark (Class 42), it had not used it at all, based on a survey of five Uni-Starbucks chain stores in Shanghai, and that Shanghai Starbucks therefore filed an application to cancel the registered trademark according to law.

Upon the application of Plaintiffs Starbucks Corp. and Uni-Starbucks, on January 6, 2004, the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court ordered evidence preservation against Defendants Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch.

After cross-examination, the parties disputed the date of establishment of Plaintiff Starbucks Corp. and the legality and validity of certain evidence submitted by the plaintiffs.

Plaintiffs Starbucks Corp. and Uni-Starbucks alleged that Starbucks Corp. was founded in 1971 and registered its first "STARBUCKS" trademark in 1976. Defendants Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch argued that the company registration documents submitted by the plaintiffs showed that Starbucks Corp. was established on November 4, 1985, and therefore its actual identity did not match its claims.

The court held: There is indeed a contradiction between the claimed founding date of Starbucks Corp. and the establishment date shown in its registration materials. The date of establishment of Starbucks Corp. should be determined based on the company registration documents submitted by the plaintiffs, which were notarized and legalized, i.e., the company was established on November 4, 1985. Accordingly, the plaintiffs' assertion that Starbucks Corp. registered its trademark in 1976 cannot be established. The defendants' objection regarding Starbucks Corp.'s establishment date is valid.

Defendants Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Nanjing Branch raised objections to the authenticity of certain evidence submitted by Plaintiffs Starbucks Corp. and Uni-Starbucks, arguing: (1) In some documents notarized in the United States, the entity making the declaration and guarantee was a third party, Starbucks Coffee Company; (2) For evidence such as trademark registration documents and company financial documents, the notarized documents were separated from the notarization certificates without any integrated marking; (3) The plaintiffs notarized and legalized trademark registration documents and other evidential materials formed outside the United States within the United States, and notarized and legalized media reports from around the world collected in Hong Kong within Hong Kong. Such notarization and legalization are not lawful. Moreover, documents such as trademark registration lists and store opening lists in the rights evidence were self-made evidence by the plaintiffs and lack probative value; (4) The information obtained by the plaintiffs from overseas websites via the internet within China constitutes evidence from abroad, and it was not notarized and legalized, and therefore cannot be used.

Plaintiffs Starbucks Corp. and Uni-Starbucks argued: (1) The notarized documents pointed to by the defendants stated: "A certain officer of Starbucks Corporation, doing business as Starbucks Coffee Company, hereby declares." Since Starbucks Corporation conducts its business activities under the name Starbucks Coffee Company, the above declaration states the fact that the declarant and guarantor is an officer of Starbucks Corporation, which is proper. (2) Generally, notarial certificates and documents are bound together, but in this case, the number of documents is very large, so they were bound in separate volumes, a practice permitted in U.S. judicial practice. (3) Starbucks Corporation holds a vast number of documents proving its trademark rights or business qualifications in various countries and regions worldwide. The plaintiffs selected important rights evidence related to this case and submitted lists to reflect the overall status of the plaintiffs' relevant rights. The authenticity of the content can be corroborated by other evidence in this case. According to the Chinese civil evidence rules, the place where evidence is formed should be understood as the place where the evidence was collected and formed. The relevant evidence submitted by the plaintiffs was primarily collected in the United States and Hong Kong and has been notarized and legalized, fully complying with the evidence rules. (4) Information downloaded from websites under the supervision of a Chinese notary is objective and lawful and can be used as evidence.

The court held: (1) Based on the relevant evidential materials and the explanations provided by Plaintiffs Starbucks Corp. and Uni-Starbucks, the entity making the declaration and guarantee in the notarized documents in the United States should be identified as Starbucks Corp. The plaintiffs' explanation is reasonable and should be accepted. (2) When notarizing a large number of documents, the parties may, for convenience or due to special needs, bind the documents being notarized in separate volumes, provided that the notarial procedures are complied with. In this case, because the number of notarized documents was very large, Starbucks Corp. bound the documents separately when notarizing them. For the separately bound documents, the notarial certificate included a list. Upon examination, the items listed in the list corresponded one-to-one with the documents being notarized, and the legalization procedures were also completed. Therefore, the above notarized documents satisfy the procedural requirements. (3) Pursuant to Article 11 of the Supreme People's Court's *Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings* (hereinafter "Civil Evidence Rules"): "Where a party provides evidence to a court that was formed outside the territory of the People's Republic of China, the evidence shall be certified by a notary public in the country where it was formed and legalized by the embassy or consulate of the People's Republic of China in that country, or shall be subject to the certification procedures provided for in any relevant treaty concluded between the People's Republic of China and that country. Where a party provides evidence to a court that was formed in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Macao Special Administrative Region, or Taiwan region, the relevant certification procedures shall be completed." In this case, given that the "STARBUCKS" trademark was first registered in the United States and that Starbucks Corp. is a U.S.-registered company with its business operations and trademark management center in the United States, it is not improper for the plaintiffs to collect evidence of trademark rights in the United States. The plaintiffs completed the notarization and legalization procedures for the evidence collected in the United States and Hong Kong, and such evidence should be admitted. For the information obtained via the internet in China from websites located abroad, the plaintiffs fixed the evidence through notarization in China, which complies with the provisions of the Civil Evidence Rules. In summary, the defendants' objections to the authenticity of certain evidence submitted by the plaintiffs cannot be sustained.

The Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court found the following facts upon trial:

Plaintiff Starbucks Corp. was registered and incorporated in the United States, engaging in coffee retail business in the United States and worldwide through company-operated and franchised stores. The date of issuance of its certificate of incorporation was November 4, 1985. Plaintiff Uni-Starbucks is a Sino-foreign cooperative enterprise, approved by the administrative authority for industry and commerce and established on March 2, 2000. Its business scope includes: coffee, teahouses (including beverages), snacks, ice cream, and catering.

“STARBUCKS”文字标识于1985年11月26日在美国进行了商标注册，核定使用商品为第21类（咖啡壶、茶杯等）。截至2003年3月11日，“STARBUCKS”文字标识还在第7、9、11、14、16、18、25、29、30、32、42等商品及服务类别上进行了商标注册，“STARBUCKS”文字及图形标识在第30、31、42类商品及服务类别上进行了商标注册，“STARBUCKSCOFFEE”文字及图形标识在第7、9、11、14、16、18、21、25、28、29、30、32、35、42类商品及服务类别上进行了商标注册。上述各类包含“STARBUCKS”文字标识的商标（以下简称“STARBUCKS”系列商标）还在英国、法国、德国、巴西、南非、澳大利亚、印度、日本以及中国香港特别行政区、澳门特别行政区、台湾地区等120多个国家和地区进行了注册，类别包括国际分类第30、42类在内的20多个商品及服务类别。至本案受理时，“STARBUCKS”系列商标在世界各个国家和地区的注册总数已近1400次，其中“STARBUCKS”商标、“STARBUCKSCOFFEE”文字及图形商标约注册600次，“STARBUCKS”文字及图形商标的注册超过100次。

The word mark "STARBUCKS" was registered as a trademark in the United States on November 26, 1985, for use on goods in Class 21 (coffee pots, cups, etc.). As of March 11, 2003, the word mark "STARBUCKS" had also been registered in classes 7, 9, 11, 14, 16, 18, 25, 29, 30, 32, 42, and other classes of goods and services; the word and design mark "STARBUCKS" had been registered in classes 30, 31, and 42; and the word and design mark "STARBUCKS COFFEE" had been registered in classes 7, 9, 11, 14, 16, 18, 21, 25, 28, 29, 30, 32, 35, and 42. The aforesaid marks containing the word element "STARBUCKS" (hereinafter referred to as the "STARBUCKS" series marks) have also been registered in over 120 countries and regions, including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Brazil, South Africa, Australia, India, Japan, as well as the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Macao Special Administrative Region, and Taiwan region of China, covering more than 20 classes of goods and services, including International Classes 30 and 42. By the time this case was accepted, the total number of registrations for the "STARBUCKS" series marks worldwide had approached 1,400, of which the "STARBUCKS" mark and the "STARBUCKS COFFEE" word and design mark had approximately 600 registrations, and the "STARBUCKS" word and design mark had over 100 registrations.

1997年9月28日，原告星源公司与星源美国品牌公司（STARBUCKS US BRANDS CORPORATION）签订一份商标保护与许可协议，根据该协议及其修订文件，星源美国品牌公司授予星源公司一项非独占权利、许可和特权，星源公司据此有权使用和再许可他人在美国（但不包括夏威夷、美国的领地和属地）使用星源美国品牌公司所有的包括商标和服务标志在内的各项财产。

On September 28, 1997, the plaintiff Starbucks Corporation and Starbucks US Brands Corporation entered into a Trademark Protection and License Agreement. Pursuant to that agreement and its amendments, Starbucks US Brands Corporation granted to Starbucks Corporation a non-exclusive right, license, and privilege, by which Starbucks Corporation is entitled to use and sublicense to others, within the United States (excluding Hawaii, U.S. territories, and possessions), the properties owned by Starbucks US Brands Corporation, including trademarks and service marks.

根据原告星源公司的会计年度报告，星源公司1999年度在中国等13个国家拥有2498家门店，公司净收入16.8亿美元，资产总计12.5亿美元；2002年度，星源公司已拥有门店5886家，遍布30个国家和地区，公司净收入32.3亿美元，资产总计22.9亿美元。

According to the fiscal year reports of the plaintiff Starbucks Corporation, in fiscal year 1999, Starbucks Corporation had 2,498 stores in 13 countries including China, with net revenue of USD 1.68 billion and total assets of USD 1.25 billion; in fiscal year 2002, Starbucks Corporation had 5,886 stores in 30 countries and regions, with net revenue of USD 3.23 billion and total assets of USD 2.29 billion.

根据因特网上及美国发行的权威刊物发布的信息，在2001年《商业周刊》全球最佳品牌龙虎榜中，“STARBUCKS”品牌名列第88位,品牌价值17.6亿美元；在《财富》杂志2001年、2002年所作的“美国最受推崇的公司”排名中，“STARBUCKS”品牌在食品服务类公司中连年排名第1位；在2002年“Fortune1000”(美国1000家最大公司)排名中，“STARBUCKS”品牌列食品服务类第4位；在2003年美国《品牌周刊》第25期所载美国超级品牌中，“STARBUCKSCOFFEE”名列快餐超级品牌第8位。在中国商标转让网（www.dealbrand.com）(2004年5月9日登录)网站设立的世界驰名商标栏目里，列有“美国星巴克”以及“STARBUCKSCOFFEE”文字及图形商标的图案。

According to information published on the Internet and in authoritative publications in the United States, in the 2001 BusinessWeek ranking of the world's best brands, the "STARBUCKS" brand ranked 88th with a brand value of USD 1.76 billion; in Fortune magazine's 2001 and 2002 "America's Most Admired Companies" rankings, the "STARBUCKS" brand ranked first consecutively among food service companies; in the 2002 "Fortune 1000" (the 1,000 largest companies in the United States), the "STARBUCKS" brand ranked fourth in the food service category; and in the 2003 U.S. Brandweek issue No. 25 listing America's superbrands, "STARBUCKS COFFEE" ranked eighth among fast food superbrands. On the website of China Trademark Transfer (www.dealbrand.com) (accessed on May 9, 2004), under the section for world-famous trademarks, "American Starbucks" and a depiction of the "STARBUCKS COFFEE" word and design mark were listed.

1999年10月，韩国知识产权局在对一起商标注册异议申请的决定中，认定在该国注册于第112类（饭店业）等9个商品及服务类别上的“STARBUCKS”商标作为在韩国驰名的外国商标。

In October 1999, the Korean Intellectual Property Office, in a decision on an opposition to a trademark registration application, recognized the "STARBUCKS" mark registered in South Korea in nine classes of goods and services, including Class 112 (restaurant services), as a well-known foreign mark in South Korea.

经中国国家商标局核准，原告星源公司于1996年5月14日、6月28日将“STARBUCKS”文字标识、“STARBUCKS”文字及图形标识在第42类进行了商标注册，注册号分别为839975、851969，核定项目均为咖啡馆、餐馆。1997年1月7日，星源公司又将“STARBUCKS”文字标识、“STARBUCKS”文字及图形标识在第30类进行了商标注册，注册号分别为926045、926050，核定使用商品均为咖啡、咖啡饮料、咖啡调味品、茶及茶叶代用品等。从1996年5月至2003年3月，星源公司还将“STARBUCKS”文字标识、“STARBUCKS”文字及图形标识、“STARBUCKSCOFFEE”文字及图形标识在其他多类商品及服务类别上进行了商标注册。其中“STARBUCKS”商标的类别为第7、9、11、14、16、18、21、25、28、29、32类，“STARBUCKS”文字及图形商标的类别为第7、11、21、25、29类，“STARBUCKS COFFEE”文字及图形商标的类别为第30、42类等。1999年2月1日，星源公司首次将“STARBUCKS”的中文译文“星巴克”文字标识在中国台湾地区注册于第42类。2001年12月，台湾地区经济部智慧财产局在一起商标异议的审定中认定“星巴克”商标为“著名标章”。在中国大陆，星源公司于1999年12月28日将“星巴克”文字标识在第35类进行了商标注册。此后，又分别于2000年2月21日、28日将“星巴克”文字标识在第42类（餐馆、咖啡馆、餐厅、快餐馆等）、第30类（咖啡、咖啡饮料、加奶咖啡饮料、咖啡调味品及饼干、糕点、面包等）进行了商标注册，注册号分别为1367394、1369000。此外，星源公司还将“星巴克”文字标识在第21、25、35类进行了商标注册。至本案受理前，星源公司又将“星巴克”文字标识在香港特别行政区于第21、25、30类进行了商标注册，在澳门特别行政区于第21、25、30、35、42类进行了商标注册。

民事诉讼证据规则第三十八条第二款规定：“人民法院组织当事人交换证据的，交换证据之日举证期限届满。”第三十四条第三款规定：“当事人增加、变更诉讼请求或者提起反诉的，应当在举证期限届满前提出。”因此，最后一次证据交换的日期即2004年9月14日为本案举证期限届满之日。由于原告星源公司、统一星巴克在其诉状中以及在举证期限届满前法院组织的诉讼活动中均明确其请求驰名商标保护及反不正当竞争保护的商标为“STARBUCKS”等6个商标，故原告在2005年1月7日的庭前听证中将其请求商标保护的范围扩大到注册于第30类商品类别、第42类服务类别的“STARBUCKS COFFEE”文字及图形商标的主张，系在举证期限届满后增加诉讼请求，原告所称将诉讼请求具体化的说法不能成立，故对于上述诉讼请求，依法不予受理。

Article 38, paragraph 2 of the Civil Procedure Evidence Rules provides: "If the people's court organizes the parties to exchange evidence, the date of exchange shall be the date on which the evidentiary submission period expires." Article 34, paragraph 3 provides: "If a party adds or changes its claims or files a counterclaim, it shall do so before the expiry of the evidentiary submission period." Therefore, the date of the final evidentiary exchange, September 14, 2004, is the date on which the evidentiary submission period for this case expired. Since the plaintiffs Starbucks Corporation and President Starbucks clearly stated in their complaints and during the litigation activities organized by the court before the expiry of the evidentiary submission period that the trademarks for which they sought well-known trademark protection and unfair competition protection were the six trademarks including "STARBUCKS," the plaintiffs' assertion at the pre-trial hearing on January 7, 2005, seeking to expand the scope of trademark protection to include the "STARBUCKS COFFEE" word and design mark registered in Class 30 for goods and Class 42 for services constitutes an addition of claims after the expiry of the evidentiary submission period. The plaintiffs' argument that this was merely a specification of the existing claims cannot be sustained. Accordingly, the court, in accordance with the law, will not accept the above-mentioned additional claims.

一、关于驰名商标的认定

I. Determination of Well-Known Trademarks

原告星源公司、统一星巴克认为：“STARBUCKS”、“STARBUCKS”文字及图形和“星巴克”系列注册商标为一整体，因此不能以时间和地域因素对上述系列商标进行割裂，原告的上述系列商标整体上在中国达到同样的知名度。被告上海星巴克、上海星巴克分公司认为：“星巴克”注册商标与“STARBUCKS”注册商标是各自独立的商标，“STARBUCKS”商标与本案无关；原告的“STARBUCKS”等6个商标均不符合驰名商标条件。

The plaintiffs Starbucks Corporation and President Starbucks argued that the "STARBUCKS," the "STARBUCKS" word and design mark, and the "星巴克" series of registered trademarks constitute an integral whole and therefore cannot be fragmented based on time and geographic factors; the above series of trademarks of the plaintiffs have achieved the same level of recognition in China overall. The defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch argued that the registered trademark "星巴克" and the registered trademark "STARBUCKS" are independent trademarks, and the "STARBUCKS" mark is unrelated to this case; none of the plaintiffs' six trademarks, including "STARBUCKS," meet the conditions for well-known trademark status.

最高人民法院《关于审理商标民事纠纷案件适用法律若干问题的解释》第二十二条第一款规定：“人民法院审理商标纠纷案件中，根据当事人的请求和案件的具体情况，可以对涉及的注册商标是否驰名依法作出认定。”《中华人民共和国商标法》（以下简称商标法）第十四条规定：“认定驰名商标应当考虑下列因素：（一）相关公众对该商标的知晓程度；（二）该商标使用的持续时间；（三）该商标的任何宣传工作的持续时间、程度和地理范围；（四）该商标作为驰名商标受保护的记录；（五）该商标驰名的其他因素。”根据原告星源公司、统一星巴克关于确认“STARBUCKS”等6个商标为驰名商标的请求，为了解决原告与被告上海星巴克、上海星巴克分公司之间的争议，有必要对本案涉及的“星巴克”等相关商标是否构成驰名商标作出判断。

Article 22, paragraph 1 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Trademark Disputes provides: "In the trial of trademark dispute cases, the people's court may, upon the request of the parties and in light of the specific circumstances of the case, make a determination on whether the involved registered trademark constitutes a well-known trademark in accordance with the law." Article 14 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the "Trademark Law") provides: "The following factors shall be considered in determining a well-known trademark: (1) the degree of knowledge of the trademark among the relevant public; (2) the duration of use of the trademark; (3) the duration, extent, and geographical scope of any advertising or promotion of the trademark; (4) the record of protection of the trademark as a well-known trademark; and (5) other factors contributing to the trademark's reputation." Based on the plaintiffs' request to confirm that the six trademarks including "STARBUCKS" are well-known, and in order to resolve the dispute between the plaintiffs and the defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch, it is necessary to determine whether the relevant trademarks in this case, including "星巴克," constitute well-known trademarks.

在原告星源公司、统一星巴克主张权利的商标中，“STARBUCKS”商标最先注册，此后形成了以其为核心的系列商标，“STARBUCKS”文字及图形商标、“STARBUCKS COFFEE”文字及图形商标均包含“STARBUCKS”商标文字。自“STARBUCKS”商标1985年在美国注册后，“STARBUCKS”系列商标在世界120多个国家和地区注册于20多个商品及服务类别上，数量巨大。通过相关权利人的经营和宣传，“STARBUCKS”系列商标或其品牌在世界范围内获得良好声誉。“STARBUCKS”商标在韩国还曾得到驰名商标保护。在中国大陆，“STARBUCKS”商标早在1996年就进行了注册。“STARBUCKS”商标与“星巴克”商标联系十分密切。根据原告提供的相关证据，“星巴克”文字中，“星”是“STARBUCKS”商标文字中“STAR”的意译，“巴克”则是“BUCKS”的音译，整体上“星巴克”是“STARBUCKS”商标文字意译与音译的结合体。因此，“星巴克”商标是“STARBUCKS”商标文字的中文对译，是“STARBUCKS”商标在华语地区的变异。1999年2月，“星巴克”文字标识在中国台湾地区进行了商标注册，并曾被认定为“著名标章”。虽然星源公司在中国大陆注册“星巴克”商标的时间略迟，但在1998年已提出注册申请，同时对“星巴克”文字标识进行宣传工作。1999年12月，“星巴克”商标经核准在第35类注册，此后星源公司又在第42类进行了商标注册。

Among the trademarks for which the plaintiffs Starbucks Corporation and President Starbucks claim rights, the "STARBUCKS" trademark was registered first, and a series of marks with it as the core were formed thereafter. The "STARBUCKS" word and design mark and the "STARBUCKS COFFEE" word and design mark both contain the word element "STARBUCKS." Since the registration of the "STARBUCKS" trademark in the United States in 1985, the "STARBUCKS" series marks have been registered in over 120 countries and regions across more than 20 classes of goods and services, in substantial numbers. Through the operation and promotion by the relevant rights holders, the "STARBUCKS" series marks or their brand have gained a strong reputation worldwide. The "STARBUCKS" mark has also received well-known trademark protection in South Korea. In Mainland China, the "STARBUCKS" mark was registered as early as 1996. There is a very close connection between the "STARBUCKS" mark and the "星巴克" mark. According to the relevant evidence provided by the plaintiffs, in the characters "星巴克," "星" (xing) is a transliteration of "STAR" in the "STARBUCKS" mark, and "巴克" (bake) is a phonetic translation of "BUCKS." Overall, "星巴克" is a combination of the transliteration and phonetic translation of the word element "STARBUCKS." Therefore, the "星巴克" mark is the Chinese equivalent of the "STARBUCKS" mark, a variation of the "STARBUCKS" mark in Chinese-speaking regions. In February 1999, the word mark "星巴克" was registered as a trademark in Class 42 in the Taiwan region and was once recognized as a "well-known mark." Although Starbucks Corporation registered the "星巴克" mark in Mainland China slightly later, it had already filed an application in 1998 and concurrently conducted publicity for the word mark "星巴克." In December 1999, the "星巴克" mark was approved for registration in Class 35, and thereafter Starbucks Corporation registered it in Class 42.

原告星源公司进入中国大陆市场后，通过特许经营方式发展经营，星巴克咖啡店连锁规模快速扩张，销售业绩亦连年巨幅上升，呈良好态势。原告对“STARBUCKS”商标、“星巴克”商标等进行了长时间的广泛宣传，并投入了大量的资金。由于“STARBUCKS”系列商标具有广泛的国际知名度，以及原告在华语地区对“星巴克”商标的宣传、使用，“STARBUCKS”、“星巴克”商标的知名度迅速扩大，已为中国大陆相关公众所熟知。基于上述事实，应当认定“STARBUCKS”商标（第42类）、“星巴克”商标（第42类）为驰名商标。

After entering the Mainland China market, Starbucks Corporation developed its business through franchising. The chain scale of Starbucks coffee shops expanded rapidly, and sales performance increased significantly year after year, showing a positive trend. The plaintiffs conducted extensive and long-term promotion of the "STARBUCKS" trademark and the "星巴克" trademark, investing substantial funds. Due to the broad international reputation of the "STARBUCKS" series marks and the plaintiffs' promotion and use of the "星巴克" mark in Chinese-speaking regions, the recognition of the "STARBUCKS" and "星巴克" marks rapidly expanded and became well-known to the relevant public in Mainland China. Based on the above facts, it should be determined that the "STARBUCKS" trademark (Class 42) and the "星巴克" trademark (Class 42) are well-known trademarks.

**Regarding the issue of whether the other four trademarks claimed by the Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake should also be recognized as well-known trademarks:** Since the recognition of the "STARBUCKS" and "Xingbake" trademarks as well-known is sufficient to provide adequate and effective legal protection for the Plaintiffs' rights, there is no need to determine whether the other four trademarks are well-known. Therefore, the Plaintiffs' above claims are not supported.

**II. Issues concerning trademark infringement and unfair competition**

The Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake alleged that the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch engaged in two types of infringing acts: (1) registering the characters "Xingbake" (星巴克) as the trade name (字号) in their enterprise name; and (2) using various Chinese and English word marks and graphic marks in their business operations.

**(A) Whether the act of the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch in registering the characters "Xingbake" as the trade name in their enterprise name constitutes infringement**

1. The Plaintiff Xingyuan Company had prior use of the "Xingbake" characters. In terms of the timing of use of the "Xingbake" characters, Xingyuan Company registered the "Xingbake" trademark in the Taiwan Region of China on February 1, 1999, while the enterprise name of the Defendant Shanghai Xingbake was pre-approved on October 20, 1999. In terms of the registration timing of the enterprise name and trademark in Mainland China, the "Xingbake" trademark was first approved for registration on December 28, 1999, and Xingyuan Company obtained the exclusive right to use the trademark from the date of approval. Shanghai Xingbake was established on March 9, 2000. Although its enterprise name was pre-approved on October 20, 1999, according to the relevant provisions of the *Measures for the Implementation of Enterprise Name Registration Administration* of China, an enterprise enjoys the right to its name from the date of its establishment. Therefore, the right to the "Xingbake" trademark was obtained earlier than the right to the Defendant's enterprise name.

2. The Defendant Shanghai Xingbake, by registering the characters "Xingbake" as its trade name, had the subjective intent to free-ride on another's well-known trademark. After the Plaintiff Xingyuan Company entered the Mainland China market, its business performance was good. Simultaneously, based on the extensive international reputation and good will of the "STARBUCKS" series of trademarks, the "STARBUCKS" and "Xingbake" trademarks rapidly gained high reputation in Mainland China. Before Shanghai Xingbake registered its enterprise name, both the "STARBUCKS" and "Xingbake" trademarks had already enjoyed high reputation in Mainland China. According to a report in the *Liberation Daily* on August 1, 2003, when interviewed, Mr. Mao, the General Manager of Shanghai Xingbake, stated that because they thought the American Starbucks company had opened over 4,000 stores and the "Xingbake" brand was good, they preemptively registered "Xingbake" in Shanghai. Therefore, it can be inferred that the Defendant was aware of the "STARBUCKS" and "Xingbake" trademarks before registering its enterprise name. During the trial, Shanghai Xingbake denied the fact of preemptive registration and provided an alternative explanation for the origin of its enterprise name: the Chairperson of Shanghai Xingbake, Zhuang Lizhi, after watching the movie *The Lion King*, greatly liked the protagonist Simba and was deeply impressed by the image of Simba sitting under a starry sky. From this, she conceived the idea and changed "Xinba" (辛巴) to "Xingba" (星巴). Considering that in business one must ‘restrain’ (ke, 克) one's rivals, she added the character "克" (ke) to form the text "星巴克" (Xingbake). The Defendant's above explanation is far-fetched and difficult to believe that the Defendant's use of the "Xingbake" characters was merely a coincidental creative idea; it also contradicts its earlier admission of "preemptive registration." Considering the facts of this case as a whole, the Defendant's act of using the same characters as the Plaintiff's registered trademark as its own enterprise trade name clearly shows an intent to free-ride on the Plaintiff's well-known trademark.

Article 1 of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Trademarks* states: "The following acts constitute other acts causing damage to the exclusive right to use a registered trademark as stipulated in Article 52(5) of the Trademark Law: (1) using characters identical or similar to another person's registered trademark as the enterprise trade name on identical or similar goods in a prominent manner, which is likely to cause relevant members of the public to be misled..." Therefore, the act of the Defendant Shanghai Xingbake constitutes an act "causing other damage to the exclusive right to use a registered trademark" as provided in Article 52(5) of the Trademark Law, violating the principles of fairness and good faith that should be followed in civil activities, and infringing upon the exclusive right to use the well-known trademarks "STARBUCKS" and "Xingbake" (both in Class 42) owned by the Plaintiff Xingyuan Company.

In market transactions, business operators shall follow the principles of voluntariness, equality, fairness, honesty, and good faith, and abide by recognized commercial ethics. The Defendant Shanghai Xingbake is an enterprise operating coffee shops and providing coffee services, and is in a competitive relationship with the Plaintiff Xingyuan Company. The trade name "Xingbake" registered by Shanghai Xingbake is the core part of its enterprise name and is textually identical to the "Xingbake" trademark owned by Xingyuan Company and licensed to the Plaintiff Uni-President Xingbake. Its registration act shows obvious malice in free-riding on another's well-known trademark and has caused relevant members of the public to confuse or misunderstand the trademark registrant and the enterprise name holder, constituting unfair competition against Xingyuan Company. Shanghai Xingbake shall bear civil liability for ceasing the infringement, eliminating the adverse effects, making an apology, and compensating for the losses according to law.

**(B) Whether the acts of the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch in using various Chinese and English word marks and graphic marks in their business operations constitute infringement**

The Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake alleged that the various marks used by the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch in their business operations, such as the texts "星巴克" (Xingbake) and "Starbuck," and the coffee cup pattern, are identical or similar to the Plaintiffs' trademarks "星巴克" (Xingbake), "STARBUCKS", and the "STARBUCKS" word-and-device mark. They argued that these acts also constitute trademark infringement and unfair competition. Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch argued that they did not prominently use the text "Xingbake" in their business operations, and their use of the relevant text and graphic marks was reasonable and lawful, thus not constituting trademark infringement or unfair competition. In this case, the Defendants used the following types of marks in their business operations: 1. The text "上海星巴克咖啡馆有限公司" (Shanghai Xingbake Coffee Co., Ltd.) and a green circular graphic mark with three five-pointed stars; 2. The text mark "上海星巴克咖啡馆有限公司" (Shanghai Xingbake Coffee Co., Ltd.); 3. The text "上海星巴克咖啡馆" (Shanghai Xingbake Coffee Shop) and a green circular graphic mark with two five-pointed stars; 4. The text mark "星巴克咖啡馆" (Xingbake Coffee Shop); 5. The text mark "星巴克特色咖啡 Starbuck Coffee"; 6. The text mark "星巴克特色" (Xingbake Specialty).

First, all the above six types of marks contain the text "Xingbake." The Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch either used this text as the trade name in the enterprise name or its abbreviation, or used it in combination with generic names of goods, etc. Since the Defendants' registration of the text "Xingbake" as the trade name in their enterprise name constitutes trademark infringement, naturally their use of various marks containing the trade name "Xingbake" in their business operations also lacks legal basis.

Second, comparing the English text "Starbuck" in Mark 5 used by the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch with the Plaintiff's trademark text "STARBUCKS," "Starbuck" has one less letter "s" and differs in capitalization. However, the arrangement of the other letters is completely identical, and the pronunciation is very similar. Since "Starbuck" is the core part of Mark 5, considering the distinctiveness and reputation of the Plaintiff's "STARBUCKS" trademark, it should be determined that Mark 5, containing the English text "Starbuck," constitutes an approximation of the "STARBUCKS" trademark.

Third, comparing Mark 3 used by the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch (referred to by the parties as the "coffee cup pattern") with the "STARBUCKS" word-and-device mark (referred to by the parties as the "mermaid trademark"), the similarities are as follows: both marks have two rings, an outer large ring and an inner small ring; both marks use green as the basic color tone; both marks have two five-pointed stars symmetrically positioned in the middle part between the two rings. The differences are: in the Plaintiff's trademark, the inner ring contains a mermaid pattern, while the inner ring of the Defendant's mark contains a coffee cup pattern; in the Plaintiff's trademark, the text "STARBUCKS" is arranged at the top between the two rings, with the lower part blank, while in the corresponding position of the Defendant's mark, the text "上海星巴克" (Shanghai Xingbake) appears, and the lower part contains the text "咖啡馆" (coffee shop). After combining the elements, the overall structure is also similar. Upon isolated observation, and considering the distinctiveness and reputation of the "STARBUCKS" word-and-device mark, it should be determined that the Defendant's Mark 3 constitutes an approximation of the "STARBUCKS" word-and-device mark.

In summary, the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch, in their business operations, used various marks containing characters identical to the Plaintiff Xingyuan Company's "Xingbake" trademark and used marks approximating Xingyuan Company's "STARBUCKS" trademark and "STARBUCKS" word-and-device mark. Their acts jointly infringed upon Xingyuan Company's exclusive right to use the well-known trademarks "STARBUCKS" and "Xingbake" (both in Class 42), the exclusive right to use the trademarks "STARBUCKS" and "Xingbake" (both in Class 30), and the exclusive right to use the "STARBUCKS" word-and-device mark (Classes 30 and 42). They also infringed upon the right to use the above trademarks of the Plaintiff Uni-President Xingbake. These acts constitute "other acts causing damage to the exclusive right to use a registered trademark" under Article 52(5) of the Trademark Law. The Defendants' acts also constitute unfair competition against the Plaintiffs. They shall jointly bear civil liability for ceasing the infringement, eliminating the adverse effects, making an apology, and compensating for the losses according to law.

**III. Regarding the amount of compensation in this case**

Article 56, paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Trademark Law provide: "The amount of compensation for infringement of the exclusive right to use a trademark shall be the profit gained by the infringer during the period of infringement due to the infringement, or the losses suffered by the infringed party during the period of infringement due to the infringement, including the reasonable expenses incurred by the infringed party to stop the infringement... If the profit gained by the infringer due to the infringement or the losses suffered by the infringed party due to the infringement are difficult to determine, the People's Court shall, based on the circumstances of the infringement, award compensation of not more than RMB 500,000." Article 20, paragraph 1 of the *Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China* (hereinafter referred to as the Anti-Unfair Competition Law) provides: "If a business operator violates the provisions of this Law and causes damage to the harmed business operator, it shall bear liability for damages. If the losses of the harmed business operator are difficult to calculate, the amount of compensation shall be the profit gained by the infringer during the period of infringement due to the infringement; and it shall also bear the reasonable expenses paid by the harmed business operator for investigating the unfair competition acts of the infringer that infringe upon its legitimate rights and interests."

The total amount of compensation claimed by the Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake in their lawsuit was RMB 1,060,000. Regarding the economic loss part, based on an analysis of the business operations of the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch over the past three years, the Defendants' profit over the three years was over RMB 2,720,000, but the Plaintiffs only claimed RMB 500,000 for this part. Regarding the reasonable expenses incurred to stop the infringement and unfair competition acts, the Plaintiffs claimed attorneys' fees of RMB 488,000, notarization fees of RMB 20,000, and translation fees of RMB 52,000, totaling RMB 560,000. Regarding the attorneys' fees, the Plaintiffs had agreed with the law firm to pay on an hourly basis at RMB 3,000 per hour. The Defendants argued that the profit amount calculated by the Plaintiffs themselves lacked basis and was not accepted. They also argued that the Plaintiffs' attorneys spent excessive time on gathering evidence related to the well-known trademark status, which was irrelevant to this case, and therefore the Plaintiffs' calculation of attorneys' fees was unreasonable.

The Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake claimed compensation for their economic losses based on the profits gained by the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch from the infringement. The profit amount was calculated based on a notarized statistical count of the Defendants' customer traffic. Although the calculation considered some factors contributing to the Defendants' profits, it was not entirely objective and reasonable as a whole. Therefore, the court does not adopt the profit amount calculated from this. Regarding the attorneys' fees claimed by the Plaintiffs, the amount of attorneys' fees falling within the scope of reasonable expenses should be determined based on the actual circumstances of this dispute. Since the profits gained by the two Defendants from the infringement and the losses suffered by the two Plaintiffs due to the infringement are both difficult to determine, the amount of compensation is determined ex officio at RMB 500,000.

To eliminate the adverse effects caused by the infringement acts of the Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch on the Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake within a reasonable scope, the Defendants shall publish a statement in the *Xinmin Evening News* designated by the court, apologizing to the Plaintiffs and eliminating the adverse effects for the infringement acts committed. The Plaintiffs' request to publish statements in two newspapers is not supported. Regarding the Plaintiffs' request to confiscate and destroy all existing infringing articles of the two Defendants, as this does not constitute a form of civil liability, it is not within the scope of trial of this case.

In summary, the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on December 31, 2005:

1. The Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch shall cease infringing upon the exclusive right to use the well-known trademarks "STARBUCKS" and "Xingbake" (both in Class 42) owned by the Plaintiff Xingyuan Company; cease infringing upon the exclusive right to use the "STARBUCKS" trademark, the "Xingbake" trademark, and the "STARBUCKS" word-and-device trademark owned by the Plaintiff Xingyuan Company; and cease infringing upon the right to use the above trademarks of the Plaintiff Uni-President Xingbake.
2. The Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch shall cease their acts of unfair competition against the Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake.
3. The Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch shall, within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, change their enterprise names. The changed enterprise names shall not contain the characters "Xingbake."
4. The Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch shall compensate the Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake for economic losses in the amount of RMB 500,000.
5. The Defendants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch shall publish a statement in the *Xinmin Evening News* to apologize to the Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake and eliminate the adverse effects (the content of which is subject to court review).
6. The remaining claims of the Plaintiffs Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake are dismissed.

Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch appealed against the first-instance judgment to the Shanghai High People's Court, requesting that the original judgment be reversed and all claims of the Appellees Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake be dismissed. The grounds for appeal were: First, the first-instance trial procedure was unfair. (1) The first-instance court repeatedly extended the Appellees' deadline for submitting evidence but failed to provide the Appellants with time to review the evidence and prepare rebuttal materials; (2) The first-instance court accepted the evidence submitted by the Appellees but did not accept the physical evidence submitted by the Appellants, such as paper cups, commemorative tumblers, and napkins. Second, the first-instance judgment's findings of fact were unclear, and the application of law was erroneous. (1) A large amount of extraterritorial evidence submitted by the Plaintiffs was not notarized at the place where the evidence was formed; some extraterritorial evidence was separated from the notarization documents, and the first-instance court's acceptance of this evidence was erroneous; (2) The first-instance judgment incorrectly found that the Chinese trademark "Xingbake" was a well-known trademark. The first-instance judgment failed to ascertain the well-known status of the Chinese "Xingbake" trademark and omitted to review the *Notice of Trademark License Contract Filing* dated October 26, 2000, which could prove that the Beijing company, the Appellees' first chain store in Mainland China, only obtained the Chinese "Xingbake" trademark on February 21, 2000, meaning that before that date, the "Xingbake" trademark had not been used domestically. The "STARBUCKS" trademark, which was not found to be well-known by the first-instance judgment, was far more well-known than the Chinese "Xingbake" trademark; (3) The first-instance judgment's finding that the Appellants acted with malice lacked factual basis; (4) The first-instance judgment's finding that the Appellants' marks were similar to the Appellees' "STARBUCKS" word-and-device mark was without basis; (5) The amount of RMB 500,000 in compensation determined by the first-instance judgment based on the attorneys' fees, notarization fees, translation fees, etc. provided by the Appellees was clearly erroneous; (6) The name right of Shanghai Xingbake was pre-approved, and thus it had legitimate rights to that name. The first-instance judgment favored large international enterprises and was manifestly unfair.

The Appellees Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake responded in defense, stating that the first-instance judgment's findings of fact were clear and the application of law was correct, and it should be upheld.

After trial, the Shanghai High People's Court confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The Shanghai High People's Court held:

**I. Regarding the procedural issues of the first-instance judgment**

The Appellants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch argued that the first-instance court repeatedly extended the Appellees Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake's deadline for submitting evidence but failed to provide the Appellants with time to review the evidence and prepare rebuttal materials. Article 36 of the *Provisions on Evidence in Civil Litigation* states: "If a party truly has difficulty submitting evidentiary materials within the specified period for providing evidence, the party shall apply to the People's Court for an extension of the period for providing evidence within that period. With the permission of the People's Court, the period for providing evidence may be appropriately extended. If a party still has difficulty submitting evidentiary materials within the extended period for providing evidence, the party may apply for another extension. Whether to approve such an application is decided by the People's Court." This case involves complex facts and voluminous evidence, and an appropriate extension of the evidence submission period was not improper. To balance the legitimate rights and interests of both parties, the first-instance court also conducted multiple evidence exchanges. After the evidence exchanges, both parties had sufficient time to review each other's evidence and prepare rebuttal materials. The first-instance court had already noticed and effectively prevented one party from launching a surprise attack with evidence. Therefore, the Appellants' appeal ground lacks legal and factual basis.

The Appellants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch argued that the first-instance court accepted the evidence submitted by the Appellees Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake but did not accept the physical evidence submitted by the Appellants, such as paper cups, commemorative tumblers, and napkins. Upon investigation, during the first-instance trial, the Appellees did not submit paper cups, commemorative tumblers, or napkins as evidence. Therefore, this appeal ground of the Appellants lacks factual basis.

**II. Regarding the issues of fact-finding and application of law in the first-instance judgment**

The Appellants Shanghai Xingbake and Shanghai Xingbake Branch objected to the evidence of the Appellees Xingyuan Company and Uni-President Xingbake. However, on appeal, they raised no new reasons. The reasoning of the first-instance judgment was appropriate, and the said objections of the Appellants should still be dismissed.

Appellant Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Branch contended that the first-instance judgment erred in finding the "星巴克" (Xingbake) Chinese trademark to be a well-known trademark. The first-instance judgment had already set forth the facts concerning the registration, use, and promotion of "星巴克," its market recognition and reputation, as well as the relationship between this trademark and the "STARBUCKS" trademark, and the reasoning in that judgment regarding "星巴克" being a well-known trademark was appropriate. With respect to the examination of the evidence "Notice of Filing of Trademark License Contract dated October 26, 2000," the first-instance judgment had already pointed out: "In January 1999... before and after that time, the plaintiff Xingyuan Company... used the 'STARBUCKS,' 'STARBUCKS COFFEE' word and design trademarks, and also used the '星巴克' words." That is, the first instance had already found that the "星巴克" trademark had not only been used in China starting from February 21, 2000, and the evidence supporting this fact was sufficient.

Appellant Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Branch argued that the first-instance judgment's finding of malice on the part of the appellants lacked factual basis. In fact, the explanation of creative inspiration given by the appellants during the first-instance trial was very far-fetched, and it was difficult to believe that the use of the words "星巴克" was merely a coincidence of creativity. According to a report in *Liberation Daily* on August 1, 2003, the general manager of Shanghai Starbucks, Mr. Mao, made statements to a reporter about preemptively registering "星巴克," from which it could be inferred that the appellants had the malicious intent to ride on the reputation of another's well-known trademark.

Appellant Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Branch contended that the first-instance judgment's determination of RMB 500,000 in damages based on the attorney fees, notarization fees, translation fees, etc. provided by the appellees Xingyuan Company and Uni-Star Starbucks was erroneous. In fact, the first-instance judgment did not simply determine the damages based on the fees provided by the appellees; instead, it set the amount after comprehensively considering factors such as the nature, duration, and consequences of the appellants' trademark infringement and unfair competition. This amount was not improper and should be upheld.

Appellant Shanghai Starbucks and Shanghai Starbucks Branch argued that Shanghai Starbucks' right to its company name was pre-approved, and thus it enjoyed lawful rights to that name. On the one hand, the "星巴克" trademark was first approved for registration on December 28, 1999; the appellee Xingyuan Company obtained the exclusive right to use the trademark from the date of approval. Although the company name of Shanghai Starbucks was pre-approved on October 20, 1999, the company was established on March 9, 2000. According to the relevant provisions of the Measures for the Administration of Enterprise Name Registration in China, an enterprise enjoys the right to its name from the date of establishment for the name it applied for registration. Thus, the acquisition time of the "星巴克" trademark right was earlier than the acquisition time of the appellants' enterprise name right. On the other hand, when Shanghai Starbucks' enterprise name was approved, it acted with subjective malice and does not enjoy lawful rights to an enterprise name containing the words "星巴克."

In summary, the appellants' grounds for appeal lack both legal basis and factual support, and their appeal requests should be dismissed. The Shanghai High People's Court, in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on December 20, 2006:

Appeal dismissed and the original judgment affirmed.

This judgment is final.
